questions.q: In the SMCRE model, what does the 'E' stand for, and how does it differ from 'Feedback' in interactive models?
questions.a: 'E' stands for Effect — the measurable change in the receiver's knowledge, attitude, or behaviour resulting from the communication. Unlike Feedback (which is the receiver's response back to the source, enabling two-way adjustment), Effect is the terminal outcome variable in SMCRE's linear flow. A wrong answer (e.g., "E = Encoding" or "E = Feedback") reveals confusion between process components (encoding/decoding) and outcome measurement, or between linear and interactive model architectures.

questions.q: A Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) scientist delivers a lecture on integrated pest management (IPM) to 50 farmers using technical slides in English. Only 3 farmers adopt IPM. Using SMCRE, identify which TWO elements most likely failed and explain why, assuming the Source has high credibility.
questions.a: Message and Channel failed. Message: Technical English slides are not encoded for farmers' language/literacy level (violates message-design principle: match code to receiver's decoding capacity). Channel: Lecture+slides is a passive, one-way channel unsuited for skill-based adoption (violates channel principle: match channel to message complexity and receiver's sensory preferences). A wrong answer blaming only "farmer resistance" (Receiver) or "poor Effect measurement" reveals source-centric bias — ignoring that Source credibility alone cannot compensate for Message-Channel-Receiver mismatch.

questions.q: Design a Message for a nutrition extension campaign targeting adolescent girls (15-18 years) in rural Uttar Pradesh to increase iron-rich food consumption. Specify: (a) Appeal type (rational/emotional/fear), (b) Structure (one-sided/two-sided), (c) Language/register, and (d) Visual-verbal ratio. Justify each choice using Receiver analysis.
questions.a: (a) Emotional appeal (aspirational: "Be strong like your role model") — adolescents respond to identity/peer modeling more than health statistics. (b) Two-sided (acknowledge taste barriers: "Leafy greens can be bitter, but...") — builds credibility with skeptical teens. (c) Simple Hindi/Awadhi with local food names (bathua, chana, jaggery) — matches Receiver's linguistic code. (d) 70:30 visual-verbal (photos of peers cooking/eating) — low literacy, high visual processing. A wrong answer using rational/fear appeals, one-sided structure, or technical Hindi reveals failure to conduct Receiver analysis before Message design.

questions.q: Compare SMCRE and Berlo's SMCR models on three dimensions: (1) Treatment of Effect, (2) Role of Source-Communication skills, (3) Linearity vs. Interactivity. Which model is more suitable for evaluating a one-time extension campaign with a clear behaviour-change objective? Why?
questions.a: (1) SMCRE explicitly includes Effect as the fifth element; SMCR stops at Receiver (decoding). (2) Berlo elaborates Source factors (communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system, culture); SMCRE treats Source as a single element. (3) Both are linear, but SMCR's detailed factor breakdown allows more granular diagnosis. For a one-time campaign with behaviour-change objective, SMCRE is more suitable because its terminal Effect element forces outcome measurement (adoption rate), whereas SMCR's focus on process factors (encoding/decoding fidelity) may divert attention from actual behaviour change. A wrong answer choosing SMCR "because it's more detailed" reveals confusion between diagnostic granularity and evaluation purpose.

questions.q: Critique this extension worker's claim: "My communication was effective because I used three channels (WhatsApp, wall painting, group meeting) — so the message definitely reached everyone." Identify the SMCRE confusion and explain why multi-channel use ≠ Effect.
questions.a: The worker confuses Channel multiplicity (reach/breadth) with Effect (behaviour change depth). SMCRE requires: Source credibility → Message decodability → Channel accessibility → Receiver attention/comprehension → Effect (measured change). Multi-channel only addresses Channel; it does not guarantee Message was understood (decoding), Receiver was motivated (attitude), or behaviour shifted (Effect). A WhatsApp forward may be seen but ignored; a wall painting may be viewed but not comprehended. The error is equating transmission (Channel output) with impact (Effect). This reveals a transmission-model fallacy — treating communication as a logistics problem rather than a psycho-social process.

questions.q: Create a novel 3×3 matrix that maps SMCRE elements (rows) against three extension contexts: (a) Digital advisory (mKisan), (b) Farmer Field School (FFS), (c) Krishi Mela. For each cell, specify ONE critical success factor unique to that element-context combination. Example: Source × FFS = "Facilitator's farming experience" (not just technical knowledge).
questions.a:
Expected matrix (sample critical factors):
| Element | mKisan (Digital) | FFS (Participatory) | Krishi Mela (Event) |
|---------|------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Source | Trust in institutional sender (KVK/ICAR) | Facilitator's local farming credibility | Expert's reputation + live demo skill |
| Message | Brevity (160 chars), actionable, timely | Co-created, problem-solving, iterative | Visual-heavy, benefit-focused, memorable |
| Channel | Mobile penetration, language support, IVR for non-literate | Hands-on plots, peer discussion, seasonal cycle | Physical access, crowd flow, demo visibility |
| Receiver | Digital literacy, phone ownership, trust in SMS | Group cohesion, shared problem, time availability | Motivation to attend, prior awareness, mobility |
| Effect | Click-through → practice adoption (trackable) | Collective learning → group adoption (observed) | Lead generation → follow-up contact (measurable) |
A poor answer uses generic factors (e.g., "clear message" for all) revealing inability to contextualize SMCRE elements to distinct communication architectures.
